title: RKE2 architecture
summary: How RKE2 assembles a cluster: systemd units, static pods, bundled containerd, config.yaml, joining, snapshots and certs.

concepts.title: What RKE2 actually installs
concepts.brief:
RKE2 is a single Go binary plus a systemd unit. Everything else is derived from it.

- `rke2-server.service` on control-plane nodes, `rke2-agent.service` on workers
- It runs its **own bundled containerd** (socket at `/run/k3s/containerd/containerd.sock`) — not the host's Docker or containerd
- It runs a **supervisor kubelet** which starts the control plane as **static pods** from `/var/lib/rancher/rke2/agent/pod-manifests/`
- Binaries and CNI plugins are unpacked to `/var/lib/rancher/rke2/bin` and `/opt/cni/bin`
- The admin kubeconfig lands at `/etc/rancher/rke2/rke2.yaml`
- Add-ons (CoreDNS, ingress-nginx, Canal, metrics-server) are installed as **HelmChart CRs** reconciled by the built-in helm-controller

So there is no `kubectl` needed to bootstrap and no chicken-and-egg: the kubelet reads files from disk, the control plane comes up, and only then does anything talk to an API.

RKE2 is the CIS-hardened, FIPS-capable sibling of K3s: same packaging ideas, but with upstream components and a real etcd instead of SQLite.

examples.label: The map of the filesystem
examples.code:
/etc/rancher/rke2/config.yaml           # your configuration
/etc/rancher/rke2/rke2.yaml             # admin kubeconfig (server nodes)
/etc/rancher/rke2/registries.yaml       # containerd registry mirrors/auth

/var/lib/rancher/rke2/agent/pod-manifests/   # static pods: apiserver, etcd, scheduler, kcm
/var/lib/rancher/rke2/agent/etc/             # kubelet + containerd rendered config
/var/lib/rancher/rke2/server/manifests/      # drop YAML here => auto-applied
/var/lib/rancher/rke2/server/tls/            # every certificate and CA
/var/lib/rancher/rke2/server/db/             # embedded etcd data + snapshots
/var/lib/rancher/rke2/bin/                   # kubectl, crictl, ctr, containerd, runc

examples.label: Getting a working kubectl on a server node
examples.code:
$ export PATH=$PATH:/var/lib/rancher/rke2/bin
$ export KUBECONFIG=/etc/rancher/rke2/rke2.yaml
$ kubectl get nodes

# and for the runtime, when the API is down:
$ export CONTAINER_RUNTIME_ENDPOINT=unix:///run/k3s/containerd/containerd.sock
$ crictl ps
examples.note: Worth putting in root's .bashrc on every server node — it is the first thing you need in an incident.

examples.label: The nuclear options
examples.code:
# stop everything and kill all containers, keep data
$ /usr/local/bin/rke2-killall.sh

# remove RKE2 from the node entirely (destroys /var/lib/rancher/rke2)
$ /usr/local/bin/rke2-uninstall.sh
examples.note: `systemctl stop rke2-server` leaves containers running — the supervisor is gone but containerd is not. killall is what actually stops the workload.

items.prompt: How does RKE2 run the Kubernetes control plane?
choices: As static pods started by its supervisor kubelet from /var/lib/rancher/rke2/agent/pod-manifests/
As Deployments in kube-system, scheduled normally
As separate systemd units, one per component
As processes inside the rke2-server binary
items.explain: This is the key difference from RKE1 (Docker containers) and from kubeadm-style clusters you manage yourself. To change an apiserver flag you edit RKE2's config and let it re-render the manifest — editing the manifest by hand gets overwritten on restart.

items.prompt: Which container runtime socket do you point `crictl` at on an RKE2 node?
choices: unix:///run/k3s/containerd/containerd.sock
unix:///var/run/docker.sock
unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock
unix:///var/lib/rancher/rke2/cri.sock
items.explain: RKE2 ships and runs its own containerd under the k3s path (shared heritage). A host containerd at `/run/containerd/containerd.sock` is a *different* runtime with different containers — a classic confusion when debugging.

items.prompt: You run `systemctl stop rke2-server` on a node. What is still running?
choices: containerd and every container, including the control-plane static pods
Nothing — the unit stops all child processes
Only the kubelet
Only the CNI plugins
items.explain: The supervisor stops, but containerd and the workload keep going. `rke2-killall.sh` is what tears down containers, network interfaces and mounts. Not knowing this leads to 'I stopped the node but pods are still serving traffic'.

items.prompt: Match the RKE2 path to what lives there.
items.explain: Four directories cover most RKE2 operational work. The manifests directory in particular is how RKE2 installs its own add-ons — and how you can ship your own bootstrap resources.

concepts.title: config.yaml and add-on control
concepts.brief:
`/etc/rancher/rke2/config.yaml` is the single source of node configuration. Every CLI flag has a YAML key; RKE2 renders it into kubelet config, static pod manifests and containerd config at startup.

Keys that come up constantly:

- `tls-san` — extra names/IPs in the API server certificate. **Set this before you build the cluster**; adding a load balancer name later means rotating certs.
- `disable` — turn off bundled add-ons (`rke2-ingress-nginx`, `rke2-metrics-server`, `rke2-servicelb`)
- `cni` — canal (default), calico, cilium, multus. Cannot be changed after bootstrap.
- `node-label` / `node-taint` — applied at registration; changing them later needs `kubectl`, not the config file
- `profile: cis` — enables the CIS hardening profile (with kernel sysctls and an etcd user prerequisite)
- `kube-apiserver-arg`, `kubelet-arg`, `kube-controller-manager-arg` — raw flag passthrough

Customising an add-on is done with a **HelmChartConfig** in `/var/lib/rancher/rke2/server/manifests/`, not by editing the rendered chart — RKE2 overwrites its own manifests on every restart.

examples.label: A realistic server config
examples.code:
# /etc/rancher/rke2/config.yaml
token: <shared-secret>
tls-san:
  - k8s-prod.internal
  - 10.0.0.100
node-label:
  - "topology.kubernetes.io/zone=eu-west-1a"
disable:
  - rke2-ingress-nginx      # we run our own
cni: canal
profile: cis
kube-apiserver-arg:
  - "audit-log-path=/var/log/kubernetes/audit.log"
  - "audit-log-maxage=30"
etcd-snapshot-schedule-cron: "0 */6 * * *"
etcd-snapshot-retention: 20

examples.label: Customising a bundled add-on the supported way
examples.code:
# /var/lib/rancher/rke2/server/manifests/rke2-ingress-nginx-config.yaml
apiVersion: helm.cattle.io/v1
kind: HelmChartConfig
metadata:
  name: rke2-ingress-nginx
  namespace: kube-system
spec:
  valuesContent: |-
    controller:
      config:
        use-forwarded-headers: "true"
      service:
        enabled: true
examples.note: The helm-controller merges this into the chart's values. Editing the HelmChart object directly works until the next restart, when RKE2 rewrites it.

examples.label: Where to look when a node will not start
examples.code:
$ journalctl -u rke2-server -f --no-pager
$ journalctl -u rke2-agent -n 200 --no-pager | grep -i error

# static pod logs when the API is not up yet
$ ls /var/log/pods/
$ crictl logs $(crictl ps -a --name kube-apiserver -q | head -1)

items.prompt: You put a load balancer in front of three RKE2 servers and point kubectl at its DNS name. TLS fails with a certificate name mismatch. What was missing?
choices: `tls-san` entries for the load balancer name/IP in config.yaml, before the certs were generated
A NetworkPolicy allowing 6443
The kubeconfig's cluster CA data
An Ingress for the API server
items.explain: The API server certificate only contains the SANs it was issued with. Add the name to `tls-san`, then rotate: `systemctl stop rke2-server`, `rm -f /var/lib/rancher/rke2/server/tls/serving-kube-apiserver.*`, start again. Much easier to get right on day one.

items.prompt: You edit the `rke2-coredns` HelmChart object with kubectl. After the next node reboot your change is gone. Why, and what is the right way?
choices: RKE2 re-renders its bundled manifests on startup — use a HelmChartConfig in /var/lib/rancher/rke2/server/manifests/
The helm-controller reverts manual edits every 5 minutes; use a ConfigMap instead
CoreDNS is immutable; you must disable and redeploy it
You must edit the chart values in the RKE2 binary
items.explain: Anything RKE2 owns in `server/manifests/` is regenerated. A HelmChartConfig with the same name and namespace layers your values on top and survives restarts and upgrades.

items.prompt: Which config.yaml key stops RKE2 from installing its bundled ingress-nginx?
items.explain: `disable: [rke2-ingress-nginx]`. On an existing cluster, also delete the HelmChart object — otherwise the helm-controller keeps the release installed even though RKE2 stopped managing the manifest.

items.prompt: What does RKE2 do with YAML files placed in `/var/lib/rancher/rke2/server/manifests/`?
choices: Applies them to the cluster automatically at startup, and reapplies on changes
Ignores them unless referenced from config.yaml
Treats them as static pod definitions
Uses them only during the initial bootstrap
items.explain: It is a built-in GitOps-lite for bootstrap resources — how RKE2 ships its own add-ons and a clean way to guarantee something exists before workloads start (a StorageClass, a PriorityClass, a namespace). Note it only applies; it does not prune deleted files.

concepts.title: Bootstrapping and joining nodes
concepts.brief:
One node starts the cluster; everyone else joins it.

- The **first server** starts with no `server:` key. It initialises etcd and generates the CAs.
- **Additional servers** set `server: https://<fixed-address>:9345` and the same `token`. They join etcd and become full control-plane members.
- **Agents** (workers) run `rke2-agent` with `server: https://<fixed-address>:9345` and a token.

Port **9345** is the RKE2 **supervisor** port used for registration and bootstrap — distinct from the Kubernetes API on **6443**. Both must be reachable from joining nodes.

The `server:` address should be a **fixed registration address** — a load balancer or DNS name in front of all servers — not one node's IP. Pointing every node at server-1 means server-1 becomes a single point of failure for registration and for agent reconnection.

The token is at `/var/lib/rancher/rke2/server/node-token` on the first server, or whatever you set as `token:` in config. It is a bootstrap credential: anyone with it can join a node to your cluster.

examples.label: The three node roles
examples.code:
# first server - initialises the cluster
token: <shared-secret>
tls-san: [k8s-prod.internal]

# additional servers
server: https://k8s-prod.internal:9345
token: <shared-secret>
tls-san: [k8s-prod.internal]

# agents (workers) - rke2-agent.service
server: https://k8s-prod.internal:9345
token: <shared-secret>
node-label:
  - "role=worker"

examples.label: Ports that must be open between nodes
examples.code:
9345/tcp   RKE2 supervisor (node registration)      servers <- servers, agents
6443/tcp   Kubernetes API                            everything -> servers
2379-2380  etcd client + peer                        servers <-> servers
10250/tcp  kubelet API (logs, exec, metrics)         servers -> all nodes
8472/udp   Flannel VXLAN (Canal default)             all <-> all
4240/tcp   Cilium health (if using Cilium)

examples.label: Diagnosing a join failure
examples.code:
level=error msg="failed to get CA certs: Get \"https://k8s-prod.internal:9345/cacerts\":
  dial tcp 10.0.0.100:9345: connect: connection refused"

level=error msg="failed to validate token"
examples.note: Two distinct problems: the first is network/port reachability to the supervisor, the second is a wrong token. The logs are precise if you read past the stack trace.

items.prompt: What is port 9345 on an RKE2 server for?
choices: The RKE2 supervisor API used by joining nodes to bootstrap and fetch certificates
The Kubernetes API server
etcd peer traffic
The metrics endpoint for Prometheus
items.explain: Registration and certificate distribution happen on 9345; the Kubernetes API is 6443. A firewall that allows 6443 but not 9345 gives you a cluster where kubectl works fine and no new node can ever join.

items.prompt: All servers and agents are configured with `server: https://server-1.internal:9345`. Server-1 is destroyed. What breaks?
choices: New joins and agent re-registration fail — the cluster keeps running but cannot be expanded or reliably restarted
The whole cluster goes down immediately
etcd loses quorum
Nothing, the address is only used once at install
items.explain: Existing nodes keep working, but the registration endpoint is gone. Use a fixed registration address — an LB or DNS record covering all servers — from the start; retrofitting it means reconfiguring every node.

items.prompt: Order the steps to build a 3-server HA RKE2 cluster.
steps: Create the fixed registration address (LB/DNS) covering all three servers
Start server-1 with a token and tls-san, no server: key — it initialises etcd and the CAs
Start server-2 and server-3 with server: https://<fixed-address>:9345 and the same token
Confirm all three are etcd members and Ready
Join agents with the same fixed address and token
items.explain: Setting up the address first is what makes the rest of it work: every node, including the first, gets certificates that already contain the LB name. Adding servers 2 and 3 one at a time keeps etcd quorum sane while it grows.

items.prompt: How should the RKE2 join token be treated?
choices: As a cluster-level credential — anyone holding it can register a node into the cluster
As a public identifier, safe to put in a git repo
As a one-time value that expires after first use
As a per-node value that must differ on each machine
items.explain: It is a long-lived bootstrap secret shared by every node. Keep it in a secrets manager, deliver it through your provisioning system, and rotate it if it leaks — a registered node can run pods and read what its kubelet is authorised for.

concepts.title: Snapshots, certificates and upgrades
concepts.brief:
Three operational rhythms on an RKE2 cluster.

**etcd snapshots.** Taken automatically on server nodes (default every 12h, 5 retained), stored in `/var/lib/rancher/rke2/server/db/snapshots/`, and optionally shipped to S3. Restore is a deliberate, disruptive procedure: stop RKE2 everywhere, restore on one server with `--cluster-reset`, then rejoin the others.

**Certificates.** RKE2 issues client and serving certs with **1-year** validity and rotates them automatically when a server restarts within 90 days of expiry. A cluster that runs untouched for a year and *then* reboots comes back with expired certs and a control plane that will not start. `rke2 certificate check` tells you where you stand; `rke2 certificate rotate` (with the service stopped) fixes it.

**Upgrades.** Either replace the binary and restart the unit, node by node (servers first, one at a time), or drive it declaratively with the **system-upgrade-controller** and `Plan` CRs — which is what Rancher does for you.

examples.label: Snapshot management
examples.code:
$ rke2 etcd-snapshot save --name before-upgrade
$ rke2 etcd-snapshot list
$ rke2 etcd-snapshot prune --snapshot-retention 10

# config.yaml
etcd-snapshot-schedule-cron: "0 */6 * * *"
etcd-snapshot-retention: 20
etcd-s3: true
etcd-s3-bucket: k8s-backups
etcd-s3-endpoint: s3.internal
examples.note: A snapshot on the same disk as etcd is not a backup. Ship them off the node.

examples.label: Certificate expiry, before it bites
examples.code:
$ rke2 certificate check
Checking certificates in /var/lib/rancher/rke2/server/tls
  serving-kube-apiserver.crt: expires May 02 2027 (243 days)
  client-kube-apiserver.crt:  expires May 02 2027 (243 days)

# to rotate:
$ systemctl stop rke2-server
$ rke2 certificate rotate
$ systemctl start rke2-server
examples.note: Worth an alert. Expired control-plane certs on a cluster that has been stable for a year is a genuinely bad afternoon.

examples.label: Declarative upgrade with a Plan
examples.code:
apiVersion: upgrade.cattle.io/v1
kind: Plan
metadata:
  name: server-plan
  namespace: system-upgrade
spec:
  concurrency: 1                 # one server at a time
  version: v1.31.4+rke2r1
  nodeSelector:
    matchExpressions:
    - key: node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane
      operator: In
      values: ["true"]
  serviceAccountName: system-upgrade
  cordon: true
  upgrade:
    image: rancher/rke2-upgrade
examples.note: The controller cordons, drains, swaps the binary and restarts the unit per node. Servers first with concurrency 1, then a separate plan for agents.

items.prompt: An RKE2 cluster has run untouched for 13 months. A control-plane node reboots and the API server will not start. Most likely cause?
choices: The 1-year certificates expired — automatic rotation only happens on restart within 90 days of expiry
etcd lost quorum during the reboot
The containerd socket moved
The kubelet failed to re-register the node
items.explain: RKE2 rotates certs on startup when they are within 90 days of expiry. A cluster that never restarts never rotates. Stop the service, run `rke2 certificate rotate`, start it — and add an expiry alert so it never happens twice.

items.prompt: Order an etcd snapshot restore on a 3-server RKE2 cluster.
steps: Stop rke2-server on all three servers
Verify that server comes up healthy as a single-member cluster
Wipe /var/lib/rancher/rke2/server/db on the other two servers
Start the other two servers so they rejoin as fresh etcd members
items.explain: The restored node becomes the new source of truth; the others must discard their old etcd data or they will refuse to join a cluster with a different history. Any change made after the snapshot is gone.

items.prompt: You are upgrading a 3-server, 6-agent RKE2 cluster by hand. What order and concurrency?
choices: Servers first, one at a time, waiting for etcd and the API to be healthy between each; then agents
All servers at once for a shorter maintenance window, then agents
Agents first so workloads move to upgraded nodes
Order does not matter as long as versions differ by one minor at most
items.explain: Control plane before nodes (kubelets may not be newer than the API server), and one server at a time to keep etcd quorum. Restarting all three servers together loses quorum and takes the cluster down.

items.prompt: Your etcd snapshot schedule is running and 20 snapshots are retained locally. What is still missing for real disaster recovery?
choices: Off-node storage — snapshots on the same disk die with the node; configure etcd-s3 or ship them elsewhere
A longer retention period
More frequent snapshots
A second snapshot schedule on the agents
items.explain: Agents do not run etcd, so there is nothing to snapshot there. The gap is durability: a snapshot that only exists on the machine you are trying to recover from is not a backup. Restore-test it too — an untested restore is a hypothesis.
